The XCPE backdoor itself. Placed in the firmware by the box maker (ODM Videostrong) and runs with system rights: it can silently install apps, run any command, record the screen and press keys. It is the core of the botnet Google took down.
ABCNexus loader: downloads and runs the botnet\'s money-making modules (ad fraud and residential proxies that rent out your internet connection).
Listed by Google next to ABCNexus as part of the same toolkit.
A dropper disguised as a system time service. Pushed after August 2026 to reinstall the botnet as a system app.
A dropper that installs the AppSalt proxy SDK, which sells your bandwidth to third parties.
HiddenView ad-fraud app, downloaded by the operators from GitHub. Clicks ads invisibly in the background.
Host app for the Fission dynamic-code backdoor.
GaGaNode / IPCola proxy SDK: routes strangers\' traffic through your home connection.

The maker\'s factory test app (BoxFactoryTest). On infected boxes it was updated together with the backdoor and has a service that installs APKs silently. Not needed after the box leaves the factory. Never open it: some boards switch into factory mode.
The checks run through the device\'s own debugging service (ADB). Open \"Connection settings\" and give the permission again; after a week unused, Android forgets it.
The connection dropped during the scan. Scan again.

The droppers change their names and install themselves as system apps through a root exploit. A system app that appears without an update is the clearest sign.
Newly installed app. Fine if you installed it.
Apps from the Play Store or that you installed yourself show up here once.
A switched-off app cannot run. A process here means something started it anyway.
The backdoor registers an accessibility service (AccessibilityKeyDetector) to read the screen and inject key presses. Only services you know should be here.
Had been switched off; switched on again
The backdoor turns off Google\'s app verification (package_verifier_user_consent = -1) so its installs are not checked.
The backdoor uses these properties to uninstall itself, stay out of the system partition and fake its install date.

The backdoor\'s spare copy is here. It sits on a read-only partition and cannot be deleted, but it is harmless: the package that could install it is off. Its fingerprint is recorded; you will hear if it changes.
The backdoor\'s spare copy is still in place and nobody changed it. It cannot be deleted but it is harmless: the package that could install it is off.
Fingerprint recorded; later scans compare against it.
Same as at the first scan; nobody changed it.
Identical to a hash Google published for XCPE
A file on the read-only /oem partition, written by the maker. Its fingerprint is compared on every scan.

The backdoor\'s spare copy on the read-only /oem partition. If com.oemservice is removed, its boot receiver reinstalls it from here. It cannot be deleted without root, but it cannot run either while the package stays switched off, which this app makes sure of. A changed fingerprint would mean someone rewrote the partition.
The maker\'s factory test app on the read-only /oem partition (see com.oem.qa).
Google published SHA-256 fingerprints of the malware. An identical fingerprint means the very same file.
The dropper creates a new folder under /system/priv-app to install itself as a privileged system app.
The dropper writes a privapp-permissions XML that gives itself the right to install apps and reboot the device.
No libseccomp_guard, libexploit or the other listed files
libexploit.so gains root through ADB, libseccomp_guard.so stops the backdoor from being killed, the others run the proxy and ad-fraud agents.
%d open TCP connections checked; none to a C2 address or the MQTT ports
System connections to port 8000 outside your network: %s
The botnet is controlled over MQTT (ports 3885–3887) from known addresses. Every live connection is matched against them.
None of the %d names resolves. Your network blocks them.
Not a sign of infection: it shows whether your network (router, AdGuard, Pi-hole) blocks the botnet\'s servers. If they resolve, add them to your DNS filter.
With Private DNS on \"Automatic\", Android may send every lookup encrypted to a public resolver such as 1.1.1.1, past your AdGuard or Pi-hole. Turn it off if you filter DNS at home.
Off. The app switches it on only for a scan.

XCPE Guard checks this device for the XCPE botnet that Google exposed, and switches it off. It needs the device\'s own debugging permission once.

1. Open \"About\" (Settings → System → About).\n2. Select \"Android TV OS build\" and press OK 7 times, until it says you are a developer.\n3. Come back here.
The app reaches the device\'s own debugging service from inside the device; nothing leaves your network. Pick the way that is available.
This device already listens for debugging. Press Connect and answer \"Always allow\" on the screen.
Turn on \"USB debugging\" in Developer options, then come back. If it stays closed, use Wireless debugging.
A small panel will stay on top of Settings. Switch on Wireless debugging, choose \"Pair device with pairing code\" and type the code into the panel.
First allow \"Display over other apps\" for XCPE Guard, so the panel can sit on top of Settings. If the button does nothing: Settings → Apps → Special app access → Display over other apps.
If the screen asks \"Allow debugging?\", tick \"Always allow\" and press Allow.
